In [[mathematics]], especially in the study of infinite [[group (mathematics)|groups]], the '''Hirsch–Plotkin radical''' is a [[subgroup]] describing the [[normal subgroup|normal]] [[locally nilpotent group|locally nilpotent]] subgroups of the group. It was named by {{harvtxt|Gruenberg|1961}} after [[Kurt Hirsch]] and Boris I. Plotkin, who [[mathematical proof|proved]] that the join of normal locally nilpotent subgroups is locally nilpotent; this fact is the key ingredient in its construction.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Gruenberg | first = K. W.
 | journal = Illinois Journal of Mathematics
 | mr = 0136657
 | pages = 436–466
 | title = The upper central series in soluble groups
 | volume = 5
 | year = 1961| issue = 3
 | doi = 10.1215/ijm/1255630890
 | doi-access = free
 }}.</ref><ref>{{citation
 | last = Hirsch | first = Kurt A. | authorlink = Kurt Hirsch
 | journal = [[Mathematische Zeitschrift]]
 | mr = 0072874
 | pages = 290–294
 | title = Über lokal-nilpotente Gruppen
 | volume = 63
 | year = 1955
 | doi=10.1007/bf01187939| hdl = 10338.dmlcz/100791
 | s2cid = 123542672 | hdl-access = free
 }}.</ref><ref>{{citation
 | last = Plotkin | first = B. I.
 | issue = 3(61)
 | journal = Uspekhi Matematicheskikh Nauk |series=New Series
 | mr = 0065559
 | pages = 181–186
 | title = On some criteria of locally nilpotent groups
 | volume = 9
 | year = 1954}}.</ref>

The Hirsch–Plotkin radical is defined as the subgroup generated by the [[union (set theory)|union]] of the normal locally nilpotent subgroups (that is, those normal subgroups such that every [[finitely generated subgroup]] is nilpotent).  The Hirsch–Plotkin radical is itself a locally nilpotent normal subgroup, so is the unique largest such.<ref>{{citation|title=A Course in the Theory of Groups|volume=80|series=Graduate Texts in Mathematics|first=Derek|last=Robinson|publisher=Springer|year=1996|isbn=9780387944616|page=357|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=lqyCjUFY6WAC&pg=PA357}}.</ref> In a finite group, the Hirsch–Plotkin radical coincides with the [[Fitting subgroup]] but for 
infinite groups the two subgroups can differ.<ref>{{citation|title=A radical approach to algebra|volume=2568|series=Addison-Wesley series in mathematics|first=Mary W.|last=Gray|publisher=Addison-Wesley|year=1970|page=125|quote=For finite groups this radical coincides with the Fitting subgroup}}.</ref>  The subgroup generated by the union of infinitely many normal nilpotent subgroups need not itself be nilpotent,<ref>{{citation|title=Group Theory|series=Dover Books on Mathematics|first=W. R.|last=Scott|publisher=Courier Dover Publications|year=2012|isbn=9780486140162|page=166|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=pOwxAwAAQBAJ&pg=PA166}}.</ref> so the Fitting subgroup must be modified in this case.<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Ballester-Bolinches | first1 = A.
 | last2 = Pedraza | first2 = Tatiana
 | contribution = Locally finite groups with min-''p'' for all primes ''p''
 | doi = 10.1017/CBO9780511542770.009
 | mr = 2051515
 | pages = 39–43
 | publisher = Cambridge Univ. Press, Cambridge
 | series = London Math. Soc. Lecture Note Ser.
 | title = Groups St. Andrews 2001 in Oxford. Vol. I
 | volume = 304
 | year = 2003| isbn = 978-0-521-53739-1
 }}. See [https://books.google.com/books?id=UytXH6rLUDwC&pg=PA40 p.&nbsp;40]: "In general the Fitting subgroup in an infinite group gives little information about the structure of the group".</ref>
